sentences: Beneath a cold, snow-covered mountain, a scholar riding a donkey has just reached the end of a bridge.
A young servant follows close behind him.
This is Seeking Plum Blossoms at Baqiao Bridge, painted by the Korean artist Sim Sa-jeong in the late Joseon period.
In the upper right corner, the artist wrote the title and noted that he painted it in early summer of the byeongsul year, that is, 1766, three years before his death.
The National Museum of Korea keeps it under the name Searching for Plum Blossoms in the Snow.
Sim Sa-jeong was born in 1707 into a distinguished family.
But his grandfather was implicated in a plot against the crown prince who later became King Yeongjo, and the family fell into disgrace.
Shut out of an official career, Sim lived by his brush for the rest of his life.
The story comes from Meng Haoran, a poet of China's Tang dynasty who never took office and lived quietly in the mountains.
Each year in early spring, it is said, he crossed the Ba Bridge east of the capital, Chang'an, and rode into hills still deep in snow to look for the first plum blossom.
Now look at the bridge.
Meng Haoran sits on his donkey, about to cross, with the boy standing just behind.
The two figures are very small, yet everything else in the picture seems to gather around them and lead the eye toward them.
Look at the landscape around them.
Low hills curl like the shells of sea snails, and bare trees with no leaves left stand stiffly in the cold.
The wavering, twisting lines of the brush seem to carry the dry winter air itself.
Raise your eyes to the top.
A great rounded mountain rises up and seems to press down on the whole scene.
The museum describes these swelling mountain shapes and restless lines as typical of Sim Sa-jeong's late style.
Scholars believe he borrowed the composition and the figures from a Chinese painting manual, the Gushi Huapu.
Yet in the rocks and trees he blended older Korean manners from the early and middle Joseon period with the newer Southern School style of scholar painting.

This way of combining old traditions with new methods marks his final years, and it influenced the next generation of Korean painters in the late eighteenth century, including Choe Buk, Kim Hong-do and Yi In-mun.
The painting belongs to the National Museum of Korea in Seoul.
It measures 115 centimetres high and just over 50 centimetres wide, a tall, narrow format that lets the mountain tower above the travellers.
Step back and take in the whole scene.
Into a frozen landscape, one man sets out simply to find a single plum blossom.
Today, think of a small joy you would gladly go out into the cold to find, and perhaps make that journey yourself.
